speechtext:

That the federal government make a national, regional and local inventory and evaluation of all its training programs and institutions to ensure that they are being used to their greatest capacity, and that these training institutions and programs be used in co-operation with those existing in the private sector so that there is better co-ordination of training in Canada.

On Monday, December 2, 1981, the Canadian Egg Marketing Agency rightly lowered the price of eggs to farmers by two cents per dozen. This was both fair and legal, and enabled pioneers to provide for their families and for themselves for the remaining years of their lives. But then they were not robbed at gunpoint by a criminal, but, nonetheless, they were robbed by the Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen), whose voice stealthily crept into the homes of these Canadians who spent a lifetime building a nest egg for their retirement, and literally robbed these Canadians of such a great part of their earnings that their families are now left in ruins, bringing heartaches, frustrations, and maybe even suicides. speechtext: Madam Speaker, my question is for the minister responsible for housing. Legislation was introduced yesterday in the province of Saskatchewan which will guarantee that no resident of that province will have to lose his or her home because of foreclosure, and this will have the force of law. Considering that the minister has made a promise to that effect at the national level, and in light of the fact there are 635,000 home owners in Canada who will have their mortgages coming up for renewal next year, is the federal government prepared to back up this vague promise with the security of law so that when these home owners go to the banks they will have a firm foundation upon which to deal?

speakeroldname: Hon. Paul J. Cosgrove (Minister of Public Works):
speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission

Madam Speaker, I thank the leader of the New Democratic Party for the question. I had the opportunity of discussing this matter with the minister of housing for the province of Saskatchewan during my visit some few days ago. I should like to point out at the outset that the move is obviously in response to the fact that fewer than 100 home owners faced foreclosure during 1981. In response to that we feel the Canada mortgage renewal plan addresses the problems which the legislation that was introduced attempts to address. Indeed, it appears as if the challenge to the courts under this new legislation will result from the equitable rules we have already applied in the plan announced in the budget.

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, my question of privilege arises from answers given by the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Cosgrove) who is responsible for housing, to questions posed yesterday by the Right Hon. Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Clark) and today by me. Yesterday my leader pointed out that the minister had told two different stories on two different occasions; today in my question I also pointed out that the minister had given two different answers on two different occasions.
I want to invite you, Madam Speaker, to consider a question of privilege which is not exactly covered by the rules. I submit to you that one of the privileges of a member of the House is to have the truth for herself, for himself and for the country. I invite you to set a precedent within the rules and to widen them. When it is clearly demonstrated to the House that a minister has made contradictory statements and when that minister refuses, when asked, to establish which of those contradictory statements is more correct, I submit to you that the House has a right to the truth.

The failure of a Minister of the Crown to answer a question may not be raised as a question of privilege.

If there is one privilege upon which all members of the House are entitled to rely, it is upon the answers of ministers being consistent.
In order to give emphasis to the matter, I am going to contrast it with an example of something that happened several years ago. In the case before us the record shows that in reply to questions put by the Right Hon. Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Clark) yesterday, the minister made one statement on the day referred to in the question and the following day made a totally contrary statement.
Questioning by the deputy House leader today demonstrates that the same thing has occurred again; one answer on one day and a totally different answer on another. In my mind that constitutes circumstances worthy of consideration as to whether they constitute a question of privilege.
May I draw to the attention of the Chair the precedent upon which I could rest my case exclusively but need not do so, namely, that contradictory statements or misleading statements to the House are matters which may be found to be questions of privilege.
I take the Chair back to a precedent which occurred in 1963 when the prime minister of the day, the late Mr. Pearson, in responding to questions raised by the opposition, stated to the House that the first he had heard of certain circumstances relating to the rather scandalous matters which arose on that occasion was when he had returned from a trip to Jamaica, I believe it was. It was only a question of having heard of the matter within the previous couple of days. It transpired, two or three days later, as the result of the work of the media and of members of the opposition, that his answer was incorrect and that the minister of justice of the day had in fact briefed the prime minister during a trip from Prince Edward Island to Ottawa. The clearly contradictory statements made by the prime minister of that day constituted a very real question of

privilege. I draw the analogy to the contradictory statements now under consideration.
After presentation of the case and a consideration of the contrariness of those statements, of course the Chair is at liberty to find that they do not constitute a question of privilege since they do not want to mislead members of the House. I submit to the Chair, however, that the hon. member who raised the question has a right to present enough of his case to the Chair to show the contradictory nature of those statements in order to at least bring it within the purview of the consideration of the Chair. What the Chair does with it after that is another question. Your Honour may well find that the circumstances about to be described do not constitute a breach of privilege. The bottom line, however, is that if a minister of the Crown misleads a member of the House, in my submission that is a very serious breach of privilege. I also submit, however, that the Chair is bound, in the protection of the privileges and rights of all members of the House, at least to hear the case in order to be in a position to make that decision.

I was interrupted by the hon. member for Hamilton Mountain (Mr. Deans) who, I thought, was asking a question by the inch and, indeed, he was. I measured it and it was seven inches long. At a minute per inch that is how much of my time I gave to him in the debate. I hope he appreciates that. I hope he sits there and listens as a result of those interjections, particularly by the hon. member for Comox-Powell River (Mr. Skelly). I am sorry he is not here today. He must be at a committee or somewhere. He was assisted by the hon. member for Hamilton Mountain.
When I was explaining that they were not going to support this legislation but would vote against it, they agreed with that. I suggested the reason for that lack of support is that the measure does not go far enough, and they agreed with that. They want to see the bill go as far along the road to nationalization of this industry as possible. That is a rather hypocritical stance to be taking.

December 9, 1981
Canada Oil and Gas Act
They asked in their interjections whether I care about the aboriginal people, and do I not care about environmental concerns. Indeed I do, but let them not be so hypocritical as to take the stance, all in support of the native peoples, that nothing should be done until native land claims have been settled in the Yukon and the Northwest Territories, and then turn around and say to the government that they want it to go further in this bill than it has. It seems to me these are mutually inconsistent stances. That is not unusual from that corner. Indeed, I often think they should instal another translation booth down there because, while their friends across the way in the Liberal Party understand their particular language, we have grave difficulty in understanding jibberish, and that is what usually comes from over there.
When I was speaking to the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) about the uranium cartel, he made some interesting statements about that arrangement. He has allowed some tiny tidbits of information to slip out in his glib, offhand way. In off-the-cuff, carefully prepared press statements he has said: "Well, we cannot let out the information because that would be contravening the combines legislation in the United States, and we do not want to have our relationship deteriorate any more than it already has with that country." But what about the Canadian combines legislation? Are the oil companies not now under investigation by the Restrictive Trade Practices Commission? Are they not faced with accusations of doing exactly what this government is doing under those uranium arrangements? None of these matters have seen the light of day. They are just like what actually happened in respect of the Petrofina purchase; they will remain forever hidden as long as those hon. rascals stay over there. Surely these matters ought to be elucidated before the House conveys new major powers on the government. This government having done the things it has done, surely there is no limit to what it will do under this legislation.
Another major consideration about this bill is the matter of self-sufficiency. Government spokesmen, one after the other, have suggested that the bill will move the country toward self-sufficiency. That is bunkum. All the evidence points the other way. The government's so-called Canadianization program has exactly the opposite effect. It has driven capital out of the country in a flight unprecedented in modern times. We have heard the accurate statistics given by the hon. members for Calgary Centre (Mr. Andre) and Calgary South (Mr. Thomson). Canadianization has forced small Canadian companies to the wall. The 25 per cent back-in clause will remove from the remaining Canadian companies any opportunity for profitable operation.
Finally, the policy pursued by this government of increasing state intervention has antagonized our friends, our clients and our best customer, the United States. The United States sees in the philosophy of this legislation, which is only the tip of the iceberg, an objective that is not financial and not economic but, rather, ideological. The government is moving on a broad front to exert its authority in every area of economic and
political activity in a way that no government in the history of this country has ever done before.
The government has interfered with freedom of the press, and it is in a position to threaten and intimidate the media with intimations of government control. The government has placed the economy in a straitjacket and destroyed the ability of the country to meet new economic challenges. The government has acted both illegally and arbitrarily in demolishing a large segment of this country's ground transportation system at an enormous potential increase in transportation and energy expenditures.
Meanwhile, in the energy field, serious problems involve bringing new sources on-stream and initiating the use of alternative energy resources. The bill does nothing to solve these problems. It merely reinforces the government's capacity to interfere, to intervene, to harass and to intimidate operators in the energy field. In the poll which was taken the other day on what Canadians feared most in this country today, 44 per cent indicated they feared big government, especially this government which is not worthy of any further trust. A government which has shown itself to be secretive, power-hungry, spendthrift, arrogant and dishonest does not deserve any new accretion of authority.
Those are some of the reasons why this bill should not be proceeded with at the present time.
I have tried to be entirely objective in my remarks last Thursday and now. My last plea is strictly a parochial plea, Mr. Speaker, and I would like the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development (Mr. Munro), who, I understand, is speaking next in this debate, to explain his way around this, that what the government is planning with this bill will deny forever the control over resources to the Yukon and any province which might be created out of the Northwest Territories. Without that control, without those resource revenues, we can forget about ever becoming a province, and that minister has been a part of that plot and the philosophy to prevent it ever coming about. Let there be no mistake about that.

If we should face the fundamental question of making provinces out of the Yukon and Northwest Territories at some subsequent time or decide that not only full and responsible government should come to the Yukon-it has almost come to the Yukon now-then-

It is for an act of volition on the part of this government and the government of the day, if it wishes to change that situation. That is the case now, as it
Canada Oil and Gas Act

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subsubtopic: MEASURE RESPECTING OIL AND GAS INTERESTS
speechtext: That is exactly what we are complaining about.

speakerposition: Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development
subsubtopic: MEASURE RESPECTING OIL AND GAS INTERESTS
speechtext:
The hon. member says that that is exactly what they are complaining about. He attributed to this bill those qualities, clearly stating that this changed the rules of the game and created a new situation in his view. Now he is saying "exactly" when I said that it did not change the situation one iota. I wish he would make up his mind.
What we are debating today, Mr. Speaker, has had a lot of scrutiny over the last year. Aside from the required parliamentary examination, it has been analysed in the news media. The energy resource industry has carefully probed it in both letter and spirit. The provincial and territorial governments have taken a hard look at it, as well as the people for whom it has very immediate and great social meaning. I am referring, of course, to the northerners, native and non-native, who realize the importance of non-renewable resource development in their future.
If I may, I would like to use the time available to me today to set forth as clearly as I can some of the broad concepts of Bill C-48 and what it is going to mean to Canadians in terms of future energy and national economic growth.
It would be difficult to view this legislation in isolation from the National Energy Program which was introduced only two months before Bill C-48, almost exactly a year ago. In point of fact, both pieces of legislation complement one another. Both are integral components of an over-all government thrust aimed at eliminating Canada's dependency on imported energy supplies and in giving Canadians greater ownership and control over their own petroleum resources.
We are all well aware of the global economic convulsions resulting from the dramatic escalation of OPEC oil prices in the 1970s, to say nothing of the temporary interruption of the supply. Canada did not escape unscathed. Indeed, many economists say that we are still feeling the effects today.
Even before those traumatic events, there was widespread recognition in Canada that our existing oil and gas legislation was outdated. It goes back more than two decades and is utterly inappropriate to our current resource needs.
The legislation as it now exists does little to spur exploration and development of new sources of gas and oil. The legislation that we wish to replace makes no mention whatsoever of the needs and aspirations of our aboriginal peoples and does not have sufficiently stringent environmental safeguards.
It was against this background that the National Energy Program was devised. As hon. members are aware, the new legislation provides for incentives to encourage petroleum exploration and production. It establishes firm ground rules as to how these activities will be conducted and by whom. It will secure for the people of Canada an equitable share in resource development. It also makes clear that no resource development will be undertaken at an unacceptable cost to the environment.

December 9, 1981
Canada Oil and Gas Act
At the same time, and most important, it provides that native Canadians must be given an opportunity to participate in and benefit from resource development in the north.

subsubtopic: MEASURE RESPECTING OIL AND GAS INTERESTS
speechtext: That is not in the bill.

speakerposition: Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development
subsubtopic: MEASURE RESPECTING OIL AND GAS INTERESTS
speechtext:
One thing that Bill C-48 does not do is prejudice the negotiation of native land claims settlements. The notion that it seeks to remove oil and gas rights from the negotiating process is simply not true. As a matter of fact, in view of the recent constitutional developments, it may be of interest to point out that Bill C-48 contains the following clause which hon. members will recognize from the constitutional resolution which is now on its way to England. It says:
Nothing in this act abrogates or derogates from any aboriginal title, right or claim that pertained to the aboriginal peoples of Canada prior to the coming into force of this act.
The government has been fortunate in receiving substantial input from northerners in preparing this legislation. Indeed, no fewer than eight of the amendments accepted by the government originated with the Inuit Committee on National Issues. Important contributions have also been made by the Dene Nation, the Council for Yukon Indians, the Metis Association of the Northwest Territories and the governments of the two territories.
One of the northern groups which expressed deep concern about the possible implications of Bill C-48 is the Committee for Original Peoples' Entitlement, commonly known as COPE. Its president, Mr. Sam Raddi, wrote to my colleague, the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Lalonde), and myself seeking reassurance that the legislation now before us would not impinge upon the agreement in principle reached late in 1978 on the COPE land claim. On December 8, just yesterday, the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources and I both signed a letter to Mr. Raddi, which I think has particular significance regarding aboriginal claims and the comprehensive claims of all the native peoples north of 60. The letter read in part as follows:
Bill C-48 does not interfere with existing aboriginal rights and specifically does not contradict the government's commitments under the COPE agreement-in-principle. More explicitly, we both confirm to you that neither Bill C-48 nor, more importantly, action taken pursuant to Bill C-48 will foreclose any element of a settlement arrived at with COPE on the basis of the commitment expressed in the COPE agreement-in-principle.
The letter went on to express our belief that the agreement in principle should be interpreted as including the 25 per cent Crown share to be created under Section 27 of Bill C-48. The Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources and I, therefore, added in the letter that it was the government's intention to provide for the transfer of these interests to the Inuvialuit in any final settlement based on the 1978 agreement in principle. This satisfied Mr. Raddi, after a history of much soul searching and unhappiness with respect to Bill C-48. He replied on the same date-that is, yesterday-expressing the gratitude of the Inuvialuit for our efforts which had, in his words, "resolved
our long-standing concern" about the possible effects of Bill C-48 on the COPE agreement in principle. Mr. Raddi wrote that COPE would like to interpret our actions as an indication of "a renewed commitment on the part of this government to honour its agreement with us". I do not think I am being overly optimistic when I look forward to the resumption of negotiations toward the finalization of the Inuvialuit settlement.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subsubtopic: MEASURE RESPECTING OIL AND GAS INTERESTS
speechtext: Are we going to be involved?

speakerposition: Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development
subsubtopic: MEASURE RESPECTING OIL AND GAS INTERESTS
speechtext:
Yes, you will be involved, as you have been involved. If the hon. member is referring to the Yukon government, I am glad to hear him talk about involvement. The position paper we are ready to put to COPE has been advanced to the Yukon for its comments before it is put to COPE. We asked for the views of the Yukon government. I cannot think of a greater expression of our desire to involve the Yukon government. I will not comment on what happened after it was sent.
The government views resource development in the north as an ongoing process involving all levels of government, including those of the Yukon and Northwest Territories, the northern people and, of course, the private sector. A prime example of this ongoing process of involving all the key elements-the native peoples of the north and certainly the governments of the north-in terms of any type of resource development is the Norman Wells oil field expansion and pipeline project. I can point to no greater example than that. Hon. members might recall that, in relation to that particular pipeline project, there was a great deal of apprehension north of 60. People were concerned that the rights of native peoples north of 60 might be prejudiced. The Roman Catholic Church, the United Church of Canada, the Anglican Church of Canada and all the major church groups expressed grave concerns about the Norman Wells project. The leadership of the entire Dene nation and the Metis were expressing severe reservations about the Norman Wells pipeline project. It became symbolic of the polarization which surrounds any development project north of 60. It polarized the entire community-or it seemed to-in very real terms into pro-development and anti-development sentiments. In my view there was no greater challenge facing any government than that particular project in terms of opening up development in the north. Indeed, the forces of polarization had to be undermined. The community and the heretofore perceived adverse interests had to be reconciled so that that project could move ahead. Indeed, that is precisely what happened. A compromise was reached. The compromise was to approve the project but to delay its commencement north of 60 for a two-year period. This received the approval not only of the Northwest Territorial government but also of the proponents-the developers themselves-Esso Resources and Inter-provincal Pipe Line. However, more important, it brought on side the very people who were most concerned about the impact of the project, the Dene Nation and the Metis. When the decision and all its elements were announced by the government, they supported the decision to go ahead with

Norman Wells. How was that done? It was an example and tangible evidence of the commitment of the government to involve northerners in every stage of the development of Norman Wells. There was a pattern to ensure that northerners would be involved in the development of the north. There was a package of joint ventures. Roughly $1.5 million were put up to allow, in this case northerners, to participate with the oil company whether it was with respect to oil rigs or other types of involvement. Over four years, $10.5 million were put up for special training to ensure that northerners participated in the actual construction of the pipeline and also in the running of the oil field. It was a management regime made up of northerners which would govern the day to day operations of the whole project. There was an advisory committee made up of northerners to advise the minister on the monitoring, from a political point of view, of the project throughout its entire history. There were social and community development moneys totalling $4.5 million put up to ensure that we could cope with the social and community fallout effects of the pipeline.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subsubtopic: MEASURE RESPECTING OIL AND GAS INTERESTS
speechtext: You did not even consult the northern government on this bill.

speakerposition: Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development
subsubtopic: MEASURE RESPECTING OIL AND GAS INTERESTS
speechtext:
What more tangible evidence can there be? Money was put up front so that the territorial government could provide an infrastructure for the pipeline. What more tangible evidence could there be of the involvement of northerners in a major project and a solution which brings on side the territorial government, the native peoples and the developers themselves than the proposal we put before them? Rather than specious allegations which have no foundation I am offering the people of the north concrete evidence that that can be done and that there was the political will on the part of this government to see that it would be done.
To achieve our 1990 goal of energy security and to maintain that position in the years ahead, an enormous and continuing capital investment in energy projects will be required. It is the intention of the National Energy Program to get Canadians fully into the oil and gas game for the first time in our history. The bulk of the necessary investment in conventional oil and gas will be generated in Canada as before but with a better balance of ownership. Some of our megaprojects such as those in the oil sands will, no doubt, require additional capital from outside Canada. Canada will continue to welcome such investments. The returns will be generous.
Bill C-48 is crucial to the development of long-term stability of oil and gas supply in Canada. The frontier regions may or may not help to meet a significant part of Canada's energy needs in the 1980s but we all hope they do, and passage of this legislation is essential if that hope is to have a realistic chance of fulfilment.
I would like to reiterate that Bill C-48 will be administered jointly by my department and the Department of Energy, Mines and Resources. With this in mind, the two departments will set up the Canada Oil and Gas Lands Administration- COGLA as it is commonly referred to-pooling the resources
Canada Oil and Gas Act
of each and reporting to myself and the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources.
This legislation is designed to take into account and be adaptable to the concerns of native people and other northerners. It is also sensitive to the process of political change in the north. Again it is in no way intended to prejudice the outcome of ongoing discussions on major issues such as land claims and the political development of the two territories, each of which is important in its own right and deserves the benefit of full discussion and negotiation.
Bill C-48 is good legislation. It is good for the nation and its economy, good for the territorial governments, good for industry and, more particularly, it is good for the people who live in the north. As such, it deserves our support.
I thank you, Mr. Speaker, and I recommend this bill's adoption by my colleagues.

subsubtopic: MEASURE RESPECTING OIL AND GAS INTERESTS
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: MEASURE RESPECTING OIL AND GAS INTERESTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am grateful that the government has been able to make an agreement with the Committee for Aboriginal Peoples' Entitlement. I am also happy that Mr. Raddi has expressed his gratitude. However, with regard to the rest of the north, it remains to be seen. I am afraid I am not going to be so kind, given the nature of this bill, to the Liberal side and other people in the country in general.
The invoking of closure is the latest testament to this government's apparent thirst for power over the Canadian north. Bill C-48 has rightly been called an unprecedented power grab by the federal government. I suppose it is only being consistent when the government tries to bring debate to a close with this type of procedural power play.
This bill remains unacceptable to myself, my constituents and all northern residents for a great number of reasons. Before I get into these in detail, I think it is important to again remind hon. members of the true significance of this bill. Only by viewing it in its proper historic context can we appreciate its potential impact on the country as a whole and the north in particular.
To average Canadians, the title of this bill makes it appear quite innocuous. It is just another bill before the House, people might conclude, but nothing could be further from the truth. It must be understood by the Canadian people and by members of the House that what we are seeing in the government's National Energy Program, of which Bill C-48 is the main plank, is a move to structure the economy in a way that is unparalleled since the days of the national policy of 100 years ago.
The original national policy was designed to exploit the resources of the west for the benefit of the dominant commercial interests in central Canada. While it contained a variety of measures designed to build up the national economy, two main elements characterized its approach to the western frontier.

December 9, 1981
Canada Oil and Gas Act
One was the securing of control over the land and the other was the building of a transportation system to ship out the resources. When we look at the government's National Energy Program and the bill that is now before this House, it is obvious that a direct parallel exists between the national policy of the 1880s and the National Energy Program of the 1980s.
The purpose of Bill C-48 is to accomplish both of these goals, only this time on a different frontier. The designation of lands in the north as Canada lands is an explicit attempt by the government to solidify its control over those areas in preparation for the development it seeks to promote.
While in the west it was the CPR that was the main vehicle for extracting resources, in the north it will be pipelines and super tankers. By securing its control over the north with Bill C-48, the government is laying the legislative groundwork for these eventualities. I regret to say that we will probably be seeing them sooner rather than later.
There is reason for all Canadians, not just northerners, to be concerned about where the National Energy Program and Bill C-48 are taking us. Since the Second World War, this government has tried to tell Canadians that the best way to overcome our economy's traditional reliance on resource exports has been to invite Americans in to build up our industrial and manufacturing sectors. Now with those branch plant operations closing down at an alarming rate and the failure of post-war economic policies becoming all too apparent, the government is once again moving to make resources, this time energy, the centrepiece of Canada's economic development policy.
There are many elements in the bill which provide thinking Canadians with cause for concern, but I would like to touch on four in particular. They are ones which I and my colleagues in the NDP have been fighting the hardest since this bill was announced in the House.
Let me review first some of the deficiencies of this bill which should be of great concern, as I said before, to all Canadians. First, the bill is being sold to the Canadian people as a piece of legislation that will lead to the Canadianization of the oil and gas industry. As my colleague the hon. member from Van-couver-Kingsway (Mr. Waddell) has pointed out time and time again, this is a complete sham. For one thing, Canadianization implies to most of us that the industry will be under the control of the people of Canada. However, this is not what this bill will accomplish in the least. Instead, it will continue to promote the domination of the oil industry by a few large companies, including the multinationals.
When the government assures us with great nationalistic pride that its goal is to achieve 50 per cent Canadian ownership in the industry, it is perpetrating a sleight of hand on the Canadian public.
It forgets to tell the Canadian people that U.S. oil companies will still be able to have majority control of the oil industry through their subsidiaries. In effect, the only thing Bill C-48 will do will be to encourage foreign firms to set up
dummy corporations within Canada to qualify for the lucrative tax benefits so willingly provided by this government.
The government is also taking great nationalistic satisfaction out of the proposed 25 per cent interest that will accrue to PetroCan. Does this represent any sort of progress when we realize that in 1945, for example, the government was taking a 33 per cent interest in Imperial Oil's activities in Norman Wells? The government would have us believe that we are coming a long way toward greater control over our own resources with this bill, but the "Mack Truck" loopholes and the gorgeous tax benefits to the major players in the industry will soon prove otherwise.
All Canadians also have reason to be concerned with the industrial benefits that will supposedly result from this bill, or should I say the lack of them? For a bill that supposedly sets the framework for national economic policy over the next quarter century, the lack of any provisions to ensure industrial spin-offs is a scandal.
In Norway it is clearly stipulated that 50 per cent of all contracts generated by oil and gas development have to go to domestic industries. In Britain it is required that 52 per cent to 57 per cent of all equipment orders have to be placed with British industries. What do we in Canada get? Only the stipulation that developers submit a plan "satisfactory to the minister" for the employment of Canadians and the use of Canadian goods and services. Flaccid criterion at best, Mr. Speaker.
If Canada is going to embark on a program to systematically exploit its non-renewable resources as fast as possible, the least we can do is to try to make sure the benefits get spread around as much as possible within our own country.
Canadians also have cause to be concerned over the potential impact on the environment that this bill will allow. First, it allows the minister in charge to completely usurp the responsibilities of the Minister of the Environment for protecting the environment on Canada lands. That is like putting Peter Lougheed in charge of aboriginal rights.

subsubtopic: MEASURE RESPECTING OIL AND GAS INTERESTS
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: MEASURE RESPECTING OIL AND GAS INTERESTS
speechtext:
There will be an unavoidable conflict of interest situation created by this, only now it will be resolved internally within the Department of Energy, Mines and Resources and the Department of Indian Affairs and Northern Development, depending on whom you believe. This can only serve to limit public information, public involvement and public accountability, and when push comes to shove, it is all too predictable where the government's priorities will lie.
What of compensation for peoples affected when the inevitable pollution occurs as a result of this government's rush to develop offshore resources? My good friend and hon. colleague, the hon. member for Skeena (Mr. Fulton) has been particularly effective in driving home the point that this bill is woefully inadequate in this regard.
The bill stipulates that people cannot be compensated for oil spills caused by the government, despite the fact that it gives

the minister explicit authority to allow such spills. It does not allow for people to be compensated for loss of future income as a result of environmental disruption. Of particular interest to my constituents is the fact that it does not allow for damages to property which is not privately owned. In short, it gives people whose lives depend on the protection of the physical environment very little protection indeed.
While there are reasons for all Canadians to be concerned with the directions being taken by Bill C-48, northerners and aboriginal peoples, such as myself, have particular reasons to be concerned. I see a smirk now on the faces across the way. I think that is why there are no Liberals north of 60. If there is a direct parallel between the national policy of the 1800s and the National Energy Program of today, what does this mean for us? Doctor Tony Clarke, of the Canadian Conference of Catholic Bishops, has pointed out, quite correctly I feel, that there are contradictions in the Canadian experience of national economic planning. He notes, for example, that:
While attempting to be an instrument for nation building and economic independence, it often results in new forms of colonialism. Economic strategies are aimed at opening up a new frontier and exploiting its resources ... The first victims are generally those for whom the frontier has been a homeland, namely, the native peoples.
With the opening up of the west under the national policy, there is no question that native peoples were the first victims. They are still the victims. Those who sought to defend their basic political and economic rights were dealt with by both the military and the courts.
Let me first deal with the process the government has used to get this bill enacted to illustrate the reasons for a lack of trust. Take the matter of consultation. There is seldom a day that goes by whereby a government representative does not wax eloquent about the need for consultation with aboriginal peoples on matters which affect them. Unfortunately, the extent to which they extol this principle has proven to be in direct proportion to their own unwillingness to live up to it. The introduction of the present bill provides us with perhaps the most shocking example of this. No single piece of legislation has ever had the potential impact on northern native peoples such as Bill C-48 will have. Yet, let me illustrate the kind of consultation that has taken place. I will read the words of Mr. Jim Bourque, the President of the Northwest Territory Metis Association, which described how he found out about Bill C-48. He said:
I did not know anything about the bill. In fact the way I first ran across it was through a friend who got it in the mail with a little note from somewhere down here saying read this, because it is devastating to you guys... but as far as government officials are concerned, no, no one has ever spoken to us.
This was part of his presentation to the Standing Committee on National Resources and Public Works on March 27, 1981.
If this characterizes the extent to which the government has been willing to take native people into its trust in preparing this bill, Mr. Speaker, what right do we have to expect that things will be any better once it is in place? I am sorry to say there is more. At the same committee meeting, Mr. David Joe,
Canada Oil and Gas Act
of the Council of Yukon Indians, described how his people were not only kept in the dark about Bill C-48, but actually deceived. He spoke of a meeting between CYI and the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development (Mr. Munro) which had taken place on December 6, 1980, shortly before Bill C-48 was introduced. The meeting was about up-coming land claims negotiations. CYI was pressing to have resource issues placed on the agenda.
According to Mr. Joe, the minister:
-suggested to us that it would be appropriate if we discussed the matter with the government of the Yukon. He indicated there was no real federal policy, if you like, that was in his mind at that point in time. It is ironic that the bill was subsequently introduced perhaps two weeks after this discussion. It is apparent, to me at least, that the government had a strategy with respect to resources north of 60. But for him to forgo the kind of discussion we would have had at the table by simply saying we do not have a strategy at this time is in my estimation certainly bad faith.
These comments merely illustrate the lack of consultation prior to the introduction of this bill. The same lack of interest in northerners' views has been apparent while the bill has been processed through the House, particularly in committee. Most of the committee's time was taken up with hearing the views of industry. To say that they have an interest in the bill would be an understatement. The time given over to hearing the views of all northerners was small in comparison. In March, when a delegation of native leaders was appearing before the committee, a motion was moved by my honourable colleague from Vancouver-Kingsway which would have had the committee seek the permission of the House to travel north to solicit greater input from northerners.
Afraid to say no, I believe, in front of northern delegates, the committee, with the consent of its members from across the floor, approved the motion. Those who viewed the Liberal members' support with suspicion had their expectations confirmed at the very next meeting. With the native representatives safely out of town, the Liberal members of the committee immediately voted to rescind the previous motion. However, I believe that the northern people have been doing their part. In our efforts to clearly define our relationship to the rest of Canada before development pushes us aside, we have put together proposals for the sharing of economic wealth and political power in the north.
In the case of the Inuit, for example, we have proposed the creation of a whole new area of political jurisdiction within the eastern Arctic, which we hope would eventually achieve full provincial status.
We have said time and again, Mr. Speaker, that we do not want to exclude development from the north; we just want it to be carried out in a way that is compatible with our own cultural and economic interests. We plan to be living in the north long after the last drop of oil has been taken out. In the meantime, we do not want our culture and environment decimated for the short-term gains of others outside of the north.
We have been invited by the government to sit down and negotiate a resolution to our outstanding claims. Negotiations to me, Mr. Speaker, imply a certain amount of give and take. So far, from that side, we have seen precious little give and a

December 9, 1981
Canada Oil and Gas Act
lot of take. Negotiations also require a certain amount of good faith on both sides. At the same time as the government is negotiating northern claims, it introduces this bill which is intended to make northern energy resources the basis for this country's economic development for the next quarter century. At the same time it is assuring native people in the north that everything is negotiable. It served notice to all of us that it intends to retain secure control over the resource wealth of the north, for the benefit of the so-called "national interest".
Since the bill was introduced a year ago, ministers of the government have been insistent that aboriginal claims would not be jeopardized by it. Recalling my comments regarding consultation, I have come to the conclusion that the more the government emphasizes a particular point, the less likely it is to be true. I strongly suspect that this will be the case with Bill C-48, regarding its implications for land claims, depending on who will be the next minister of Energy, Mines and Resources.
One of the most critical elements in any land claim negotiation is the question of ownership and control of nonrenewable resources. The Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Lalonde) has said to me in the past that Bill C-48 will not preclude anything in the way of settlement. He assures us that anything is possible and that the current legislation can always be changed to accommodate whatever is negotiated in the way of settlement in the future. However much I would like to believe him on this-and I hope he is right-I am afraid that the hon. minister is moving into the theoretical plane when he makes such remarks.
The government has been eager to offer aboriginal peoples assurances that the bill will not affect their claims. It says that it even has legal opinions to back up this belief. But when the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development was asked in the House to present those legal arguments so that those who are skeptical can be reassured, he has refused to do so. If the legal opinions, in fact, support the government's contention, why should they have to be hidden and what does he have to lose by sharing them with us? One would think that it would be to his and his government's advantage if those legal opinions existed. In fact, his determination to withhold them speaks volumes about what must really be at stake for aboriginal peoples with the passage of this bill.
Throughout all of my remarks, Mr. Speaker, I have tried to draw the parallels between the National Energy Program of today and the national policy of the 1800s. I should like to conclude my remarks by again alluding to that parallel and say, if I may take liberties with the words of Frank Underhill, a noted historian, that "What this country needs is the moral equivalent of Bill C-48".

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, once again I have an opportunity to participate in this debate on Bill C-48, the Canada oil and gas act.

subsubtopic: MEASURE RESPECTING OIL AND GAS INTERESTS
speechtext: You are one of the few Liberals who is interested.

subsubtopic: MEASURE RESPECTING OIL AND GAS INTERESTS
speechtext:
The main thrust of this piece of legislation was perhaps best summarized by the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Lalonde) when he appeared before the committee, and subsequently when he spoke in the House. He noted the thrust of this legislation, and I think it is worth quoting him when he said:
It is a key element of the National Energy Program. It will provide the framework far the careful management and successful development of the huge oil and gas potential of the Canada lands for many decades. And it will at the same time secure for the people of Canada an equitable share in that development while helping to ensure that it is carried out in a safe and environmentally-acceptable manner.
That is the thrust of Bill C-48, put very succinctly.
Before I go on to the substantive part of the legislation, I should like to deal with the process which has culminated in the bill coming to a vote.
There have been many opportunities for Members of Parliament to examine the legislation. In fact, we have been dealing with it for approximately one year. My colleagues and I have never objected to the lengthy and detailed scrutiny to which the legislation has been subjected; in fact, we have welcomed it. All Members of Parliament have had an opportunity to speak to the issues, to propose amendments and to vote on the bill at its various stages. In fact, to date 235 speeches have been made on this piece of legislation. The Standing Committee on National Resources and Public Works held hearings and considered amendments to the bill for approximately six months. During those deliberations, 140 witnesses were called to testify and some 70 meetings, lasting a total of approximately 130 hours, were held. Hundreds of amendments offered by all political parties were considered and over 100 were accepted by the government.
It is worth noting who the witnesses were. There were numerous representatives of the oil and gas industry, various witnesses from related industries and individuals from the academic community. We also heard the views, oral and written, of representatives of Canada's original peoples as well as elected representatives of the territorial governments. We heard submissions and various assertions presented by Members of Parliament from all three political parties. We heard the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources and the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development (Mr. Munro), as well as officials from the Department of Energy, Mines and Resources, the Department of Fisheries and Oceans and the Department of Indian Affairs and Northern Development.
I think it is worth reflecting for a few moments on who the witnesses were, and I think we should congratulate those who appeared before the committee and offered frank and, in many instances, helpful suggestions on how to make a good bill better.
The bill was in committee twice as long as the Foreign Investment Review Act and three times as long as the Banks and Banking Law Revision Act. The committee reported this bill to the House and debate resumed for several days in July. Since we resumed sitting in October, Bill C-48 has been the sole subject for consideration, with the exception of the Consti-

tution and the economy. We have been plodding painfully through 57 motions to amend the bill further. I remind hon. members that all of these motions were considered by the Standing Committee on National Resources and Public Works.
There are times when governments have the luxury of prolonged contemplation. There are times when governments can allow for prolonged and wide-ranging discussion, but ultimately the time for action and decision arrives. Canadians demand it. Canada's energy situation demands it, and I suggest the time is now. The motion before us today challenges this House to act. Let us not avoid this responsibility which is bestowed upon all Members of Parliament who are the representatives of the people of Canada.
Perhaps not every member of the House accepts every word of every section of the bill as it now stands. But every member of the House will acknowledge that the need for this legislation is great and that the time for implementation of this new regime is long overdue. The legislation which this bill will replace is over two decades old and utterly inappropriate to our resource needs today. This legislation does little to spur exploration and development of new sources of oil and gas, makes no mention of the aspirations of aboriginal peoples, and does not have sufficiently stringent environmental safeguards. I suggest that is perhaps one of the most important, substantive portions of the bill.
The urgency of this situation was recognized by a previous minister of energy, who attempted to replace this outmoded legislation in 1971. Unfortunately, that bill died on the Order Paper. The need for a comprehensive new regime governing the offshore areas and the frontier has been recognized by prominent members of the opposition as well. The argument was put quite succinctly by the hon. member for Etobicoke Centre (Mr. Wilson) who said in Parliament on December 11, 1980:
The broad objectives of this legislation are worthwhile and certainly acceptable. One might go so far as to say that they are motherhood; they are intended to increase production and Canadian ownership, as well as to provide a very stable tax environment. I agree with the minister when he says that it is important to have this legislation. We have been waiting for it for about ten years now.
After criticizing the government for not bringing this legislation forward promptly, little did I suspect that a bill which the hon. member describes as important, and indeed, even as motherhood, would face prolonged obstruction and opposition procrastination for almost one year.
We on this side of the House have been very active. Members of the Standing Committee on National Resources and Public Works had an opportunity to travel to western Canada, although I admit the travel was limited. While there we had an opportunity to meet with the various sectors of the oil and gas industry, with some native persons and with some academics. I think it can be said that members of the committee from all parties became aware of the concerns of the people of western Canada in regard to Bill C-48.
Canada Oil and Gas Act
In addition to the trip that the committee made out west, a number of members on this side of the House made a special journey to western Canada on their own time and at their own expense, to meet with additional individuals. We were given further information and were brought up to date on how these measures will affect people out there. I think that has had a tremendous influence on what is contained in the bill now before us.
Over the same year, we made significant progress on most aspects of our ambitious and comprehensive National Energy Program. As opposition parties demanded, we have achieved new oil and gas accords with the producing provinces of Saskatchewan, Alberta, and British Columbia. We have also begun serious negotiations with Newfoundland, Nova Scotia and British Columbia concerning offshore resources. Finally, we have established an attractive price for new oil from Canada lands which, taken in conjunction with the petroleum incentives program, will stimulate new exploration and production.
How can Members of Parliament justify their efforts to delay a bill which will encourage greater Canadian participation in the petroleum industry operating on Canada lands? The Conservative government of Alberta supports the Canadi-anization provisions of the National Energy Program. The Social Credit government of British Columbia supports the Canadianization provisions of the National Energy Program. The NDP government of Saskatchewan supports the Canadianization provisions of the National Energy Program. Moreover, judging by their acquisitions of Suncor shares, I suggest that the big blue machine in the province of Ontario supports the Canadianization provisions as well.
Finally, 84 per cent of Canadians support our government's Canadianization policy, as indicated in an opinion survey sponsored by the Canadian Petroleum Association.
I suggest that Conservative members of this House need to confer with their Conservative colleagues in Alberta. The New Democratic Party, which I have often referred to as the pink rump, should also consult with their friends in Saskatchewan. They will learn, as other Canadians have learned, that Canadianization is welcomed and, indeed, is an essential part of a national energy program.
I wish that opposition members would feel the same sense of accomplishment and achievement as I do. A decision which hon. members opposite have taken was well described by the hon. member for Comox-Powell River (Mr. Skelly) in his speech to this House on October 19, when he said: "We had to resort to a filibuster and to delaying tactics. This was hard on everyone, including government members who had to sit and listen". We all know of occasions where the opposition deliberately obstructs the work of Parliament, but rarely do hon. members boast of it so openly and brazenly.
Today I wish to tell the hon. member that we cannot sit and listen forever. We have not been elected to Parliament to provide him or his party with an audience, merely to sit and

December 9, 1981
Canada Oil and Gas Act
listen, as he puts it. We have a responsibility to protect Canadians from the dangers of a volatile world energy situation. This responsibility requires action, not indecision. Both opposition parties have contributed to the delay of this bill. More than 120 hon. members have spoken on this bill in Parliament. The incurable disease I call PetroCan paralysis, a disease which numbs Conservative thinking and paralyses Conservative action, has spread from this aspect of Conservative energy policy to include all aspects.

This delay is shocking ... It is irresponsible to expect companies to operate in an environment when they have no idea what the ground rules will be... This delay... going back to 1970, has cost Canada valuable years in reaching oil self-sufficiency. It is important that we get on with the job now.
From the start, we recognized the need for long, intensive and comprehensive consideration of Bill C-48 in all its challenging complexity. We have also allowed for the necessary time to debate this bill, and more. We have demonstrated the high degree of flexibility appropriate for such a bill. We have accepted advice regarding amendments from a variety of sources. I think it important that we recognize the contribution of all Members of Parliament, particularly those in the National Resources and Public Works Committee. In addition, we should single out two persons, the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. MacLar-en), as well as the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources himself, for demonstrating that high degree of flexibility and receptiveness to changes as they relate to amendments to the bill.
I must say that we are not grateful for the hindrance we have also received from some quarters in this House at certain points in the process. At this late stage, we do not accept the prospect of further undue delay. The process is now drawing to a close, a close which is every bit as necessary as the preceding stages of consideration which have assisted so much in making a good bill better.
As I have already suggested to hon. members, we are not talking of a process lasting one year to date, but one lasting more than ten years since notice was served of the intention to update this legislation. In neither the specific case of Bill C-48 nor in the longer-term search for a new regulatory regime for the Canada lands can hon. members make a serious case for being the victims of unseemly haste.
In the final analysis, the test of whether and when this bill should be passed is not that we have fulfilled a need for full and fair consideration. The real test is the content of the bill itself. This bill passes this test at every crucial point in the challenge of meeting Canada's energy needs for the next ten years and beyond.
We have heard a great deal about the number of witnesses who appeared and the amount of time Members of Parliament spent on this particular piece of legislation. However, I want very briefly to touch on a few amendments and proposals which were made in committee by hon. members opposite and on this side. An amendment was proposed to change the definition of "significant discovery", in that particular section to read:
"significant discovery" means the first well on a geological feature that indicates by flow testing the existence of hydrocarbons in that feature and, having regard to geological and engineering factors, indicates the existence of an accumulation of hydrocarbons that has potential for production.

This particular provision has great significance for Canada, because if we are to rid ourselves of the label of a have-not province, or the have-not provinces, we will have to take advantage of that opportunity which is about to come in the oil and gas industry so that we can provide meaningful employment to the people in Atlantic Canada and they, too, like other Canadians, will have an opportunity to build homes, raise families, and prosper in society.
In addition to this particular provision, I have referred to the Canadianization provisions. The minister has included, in this particular bill, a provision in Section 5(6) whereby advisory bodies can be set up at his discretion. This is important because in the administering of this particular act there would be situations where it may be necessary to consult with certain people in the industry, to consult with various native groups, fishermen or what have you, to make certain that the provisions of the bill are being carried out with the intent that we all know.
The final comment that I would like to make in terms of the substantive portion of the bill concerns the absolute liability provisions. As an hon. member from Atlantic Canada, I am very pleased that that particular section dealing with the claims which may or may not be made by fishermen is written
December 9, 1981

in the way it is. The absolute liability regime where no proof of fault or negligence is required to establish liability is indeed a far-reaching measure. Closer examination of the relative provisions, however, will reveal that the liability under the bill applies regardless of whether this bill is authorized or unauthorized. For Your Honour's edification, that was a particular point which I think all hon. members would agree had to be clarified, and I am happy to say that it has been clarified to the satisfaction of all hon. members.
The liability provisions include not only damages resulting from spills, but also compensation for damages resulting from debris on the ocean floor. Another significant feature of the liability and compensation scheme is the inclusion of loss of income, including future income, in the definition of actual loss or damage. I must emphasize that this provision goes beyond the basis for the award of damages under the common law and, in my view, is unprecedented in any similar type of legislation.
Bill C-48 is crucial to the development of long-term stability of oil and gas supply in Canada. The frontier regions may or may not help to meet a significant part of Canada's energy needs in the 1980s, but I believe all hon. members hope they will. Passage of this legislation is essential if that hope is to have a chance of realization. However, we know the longer future of oil and gas development in Canada lies in our untapped frontier regions where the bulk of our conventional oil and gas resources are projected to be found. The time for making that future possible is now. That is why the regulatory stability to be provided by Bill C-48 is so essential at this time. There is an enormous, emerging momentum building up for exploration in the frontier. With the help of Bill C-48 and a number of supporting initiatives in the National Energy Program, we will soon see this tremendous potential being harnessed at precisely the optimum moment in our history.
The National Energy Program provides an opportunity for Canadians to begin to participate in the development of their own oil and gas resources on a grand and growing scale. That is the only scale of participation sufficient to ensure that the benefits of frontier oil and gas development are sufficiently great for Canadians to justify the high costs of this undertaking. I need hardly add that a major share for Canadians in frontier oil and gas opportunities is also essential to the goal of fairness in sharing the benefits of petroleum industry growth. Canadians are more than ready to do this job in co-operation with those companies, mostly foreign owned, which currently hold the bulk of the promising acreage in the frontier.
Bill C-48 and supporting national energy initiatives provide a regime second to none in the world for both Canadian and foreign investors to build a truly outstanding store of usable energy and energy wealth, for themselves and indeed for all Canadians.
Members of this House know that the goal of enhancing Canadian participation in frontier oil and gas opportunities could hardly command a greater degree of public support.
Canada Oil and Gas Act
Hon. members also know, indeed they have told us repeatedly, that the existing regime for frontier oil and gas was simply not getting the job done either for Canadian participation or supply development.
I believe the need to act expeditiously will be apparent to anyone with a real desire to see Canada begin facing the frontier oil and gas challenge in full measure. That is why I have not the slightest hesitation in supporting a measure necessary to ensure that this bill is carried forward in an efficient manner with all due regard to both the responsibilities of this House and the energy needs of the nation. The time is now.
