Madam Speaker, I am pleased to speak during the final moments of debate on Bill C-48. I believe the two main points that should be discussed have been identified by the previous speaker. The discussion has to centre on both the mechanism of closure and also some of the aspects of the substance of Bill C-48.
Before getting into those two major points, I want to spend a little time on points made by earlier speakers, particularly those contained in the speech made by the hon. member for Cape Breton-East Richmond (Mr. Dingwall). He mentioned Canadianization. It should be very clear to people across Canada that the Progressive Conservative Party strongly supports Canadianization. What we have a great deal of difficulty with are the types of measures in this bill and the types of things that have been done so far by this government opposite which do not represent Canadianization but represent, or may represent, nationalization, more government involvement, more interference and more difficulties down the road in terms of developing our industry.
Just as an example of the kind of difficulties that can occur, I will mention Petrofina because that company has been referred to today. I can think of a case in my own constituency concerning Petrofina. An honest dealer who works for another oil company wanted to start up a gas station. He bought land, part of which was owned by Petrofina. This dealer cannot now open up a gas station because Petro-Canada has control of the land. The dealer has asked for release, and there is not another gas station in the area and they will not give him the release. Therefore, this dealer has been prevented by Petro-Canada from earning a living on the basis of the Petrofina purchase. This is just one example. There can be more of these sorts of things as we see more and more direct government involvement through Crown corporations. This should be of real concern to all Canadians.
I believe the previous speaker repeatedly mentioned closure and he ended his speech with the words "The time is now." There would be no argument from this side of the House that it is high time that legislation be brought in to deal with programs that have occurred in the oil and gas industry, but that is not the point. The question is, what changes should be made? The hon. member made reference to the red rump. We in this party make many references to the red rump. We identify them as the red rump of the sheep on the other side of the House. I just point that out because I want it to be clear.

December 9, 1981
Canada Oil and Gas Act
The hon. member for Nunatsiaq (Mr. Ittinuar) mentioned the potential impact this bill will have on the people north of 60. I think the impact with which we are faced will affect people on the east coast, the west coast and all across Canada. We share his concern about the potential impact this bill will have on all Canadians.
I will turn now to the comments made by the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development (Mr. Munro). He had about five major points. The most telling one was the denial he made that this bill in itself represents in any way an infringement on the fundamental rights of Canadians or Canadian companies to own property. There can be no argument that this bill and its main impact with its retroactive 25 per cent back-in provision on Canada lands leased by oil and gas companies represents an infringement on the ability of Canadians and Canadian companies to own property. This kind of thing is in keeping with the general tone of government policy today, and it is something to which I will return in a few moments.
The second point made by the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development concerned existing legislation. It should be pointed out to the Canadian public, and it should be clear to the Liberal Party that forms the government, that governments in power since the oil embargo of 1973 have not reacted properly when it was clear that major changes were needed. It was the responsibility of Liberal governments to make changes to legislation. It is their fault that we are now faced with a crisis. They are now saying that they can use this bill as a justification and a rationalization for closure.
The Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development said that this bill in some way will help to provide Canadians with an equitable share of the oil and gas industry. But what it has done is provide the Liberal government with the major return. Canadians are faced with terrific increases in prices across the board for heating oil and gasoline. There is another 50 cents that will be added in the coming year. Canadians are not the ones who are getting an equitable share. The Canadian government is because of its profligate ways and its horrendous borrowing, the Liberal government having had to raise revenue. The Liberal government is the major beneficiary of this so-called equity.
As a result of recent changes in oil and gas prices, the revenue from a barrel of oil is divided as follows: the federal government receives $18.50, the Ontario government receives $8.32 and the Alberta government receives $7.56. Who is paying all this money? The Canadian public. But the federal government reaps the major benefit.
The minister talked about protection of the environment. I believe he talked in a very supportive way of the legislation and the fact that it would provide the safeguards and make sure the environment was respected. At the same time, he neglected to talk about the discretionary powers and the track record of this government in terms of environmental protection. The most glaring example is the government's effort in Toronto to remove radioactive soil and dump it in the Camp Borden area. That is the kind of environmental sensitivity this
government has, and this is the kind of thing we have to be concerned about when we look at the protection the environment might have under this type of legislation, particularly in view of the discretionary powers of the minister.
Finally, the major point he was trying to make was that this bill would in a major way help to achieve energy self-sufficiency. The goal of energy self-sufficiency was first established by the Progressive Conservative Party in 1979. This was a policy the whole country could relate to, one the importance of which is known to the people. In fact, we did not have an energy policy in Canada until that government made this a major goal. We had not had the need for energy self-sufficiency in this country identified until that time. That was a goal we established. It is a goal that the party and the government opposite are now the beneficiaries of, and it is one I think we all hoped we could achieve.
The fact is that the mechanism for achieving this goal is something that will not only be avoided by this kind of bill, but it is something which is continually thwarted by a number of measures brought in by this government, the most recent of which is the budget. I will return to that in a moment with figures to show where we will be in energy self-sufficiency with our shortfall. This bill clearly is not going to help satisfy any of those goals. In fact, it has had a net negative effect.
I should like to return for a moment to the background of the conditions we are now facing as we look at this bill. Bill C-48 is certainly one of the flagships of the government's National Energy Program. If we want to consider an example of government flagships, and we had time, we could think about the Canadian navy and how well the flagships of government activity in that field have served us. The dedication the government has given the Department of National Defence in its support for that department over the last number of years does not speak well for this measure if it is to be the flagship of the National Energy Program.
We have had at least 13 years of successive Liberal government policies in relation to energy and the economy which have today put our country into a situation which everyone knows compares only to that of about 30 years ago. We are experiencing a most severe recession, and statistics revealed today show that it will probably be worse next year. That is the kind of thing nobody likes to hear. It is the kind of thing that is entirely unnecessary, but it is the consequence of the policies of successive Liberal governments.
It is difficult for members of this party to accept the kind of promise made by the party opposite at election time. That government has made promises in respect of cheap gas, cheap heating oil and lower interest rates. All those promises have proved to be like the promise in respect of wage and price controls. They were promises made in order to get elected but never kept. This government goes on in ways which get us into deeper and deeper trouble.
The economic climate of this country is certainly depressed, and it is depressing to talk about it. The fact is that those
December 9, 1981

people who are now unemployed and those who face the loss of their jobs in the coming year must know that this Liberal government is responsible, and that as a country there is no need for our being in this situation. It is not necessary because, since Canada became a nation, we have had the resources and the opportunity to move ahead. What we have not had is the kind of direction needed to maximize the potential to put us in the position of having full employment, and the energy security, optimism and hope for the future which I think all Canadians deserve.
I should like to turn now to the mechanism of closure. I guess the most dramatic use of the mechanism of closure I have experienced was last summer when we sat here in the House of Commons in an effort to achieve in some way a quick and effective resolution to the Post Office strike. At that time, as the opposition was mounting pressure on the government to get something done to achieve a conclusion to that situation, this government brought in closure. We wanted a conclusion to that strike whether that meant legislation, which this party would have supported, or something else. The government has legislated postal workers back to work in the past. We wanted that conclusion even if it meant taking away the right to strike from essential services, something which I think all Canadians would support. What this government chose to do, at a time when business was reeling from the pressure of high interest rates, when small businesses were going bankrupt and faced a total loss of $3 billion, was to bring in closure. Perhaps it was because the weather was too hot outside and therefore we were still sitting in the House of Commons, but whatever the reason this House used closure and prevented us from terminating that Post Office strike.
This government has actually brought in closure nine times since 1979. One occasion when it brought in closure before last summer which strikes me as being dramatic was after two weeks of debate on the Constitution. At that time the government felt it was justified in using that measure. I do not know how the comments of the previous speaker related to that time, that period of two weeks when we were considering an entirely new constitutional framework for Canada. I do not know how hon. members opposite can justify, rationalize or square the use of that measure with the people of Canada. I do not know how individual members of the Liberal Party can go back to their constituencies and justify the government's continual use of this mechanism which in fact overrides the democratic principles upon which this House functions. I think this was expressed best by the hon. member for Calgary West (Mr. Hawkes) a couple of days ago. He said that members opposite will have to justify this use of closure by the government in relation to important national issues; they will have to justify overriding the democratic process of this House of Commons.
Perhaps another use of closure that will come to the minds of many Canadians was during the pipeline debate. In that regard it was interesting to hear the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Lalonde) make an announcement, as a result of a question in the House by one of his own members, about the passage by the United States government of meas-
Canada Oil and Gas Act
ures which will in fact secure the ongoing development of this pipeline. The thing that surprised us on this side of the House is that hon. members opposite should have been so relieved. We had so many guarantees for so long regarding the construction of this pipeline that there seemed to be no problem, at least to us on this side of the House. For that reason it was with a little bit of confusion that we received that announcement through the efforts of that Liberal backbencher. Perhaps the minister had a reason for making this announcement today, in spite of the fact that he has given us repeated assurances that everything was A-OK.
As this program is part of the ongoing implementation of Bill C-48, I think the initial reaction to the total program by different sectors in varying regions of Canada was that it had some favourable measures. Canadians from central Canada were among the first to give their initial reaction to this bill and they indicated that, on the basis of the National Energy Program, they expected energy security and less expensive oil and gas. They anticipated an end to the difficulties which had existed for several years in trying to negotiate agreements between the federal government and the provinces. I cannot speak for the people of Quebec but it appeared to be a beneficial program according to the people of Ontario. I believe this same attitude was reflected as well in eastern Canada.
However, the realization evolved that this program was not going to solve all the problems. In fact, more problems were created which became evident by the fact that it took at least another year to reach an energy pricing agreement. When that agreement was reached last fall, the consequences were entirely different from what most people in central Canada had originally hoped for.
I think the government has done a very wise thing politically by selling to the Canadian public all of the ingredients of this legislation under the name of Canadianization and presenting it as a single package. It is a complex and difficult issue to understand, and to present it in the name of Canadianization is a term which is very well accepted. Hon. members opposite know that this party strongly supports the intent of the word "Canadianization".
As far as the reaction of industry and the people at large in western Canada to the National Energy Program is concerned, I believe that their awareness of the consequences was much greater. Their appreciation of the results and their concern for some of its difficulties was greater initially.
In many ways, some of their fears and concerns were proven to be valid because the minister had to make adjustments to some of the provisions in order to accommodate the realities in terms of prices which would help the industry survive. These changes were necessitated by the increasing number of rigs and workers leaving Canada because they could not function in an uncertain environment, one in which there was not a guaranteed return on their investment. I think this was a major factor the minister had to deal with in terms of making

adjustments which were reasonably equitable to the country as a whole.
I would like to talk about the initial reaction to this program by the industry. For example, the executive of TransCanada PipeLines wanted to see the implementation of the more favourable parts of the National Energy Program and thought that the program as a whole was legitimate in terms of the country trying to develop a sense of national identity, that it was not something which needed to be feared but needed to be developed. It is clear from recent public submissions made by executives of TransCanada PipeLines that some of their worst fears, which were not initially revealed, had been realized. They now know that the net impact of the National Energy Program has been negative and will continue to be so unless more adjustments are made to it. There are other examples which I will not go into right now.
I would like to discuss further the self-sufficiency aspect of this National Energy Program by quoting what Woods, Gordon have to say about the effect of the National Energy Program and self-sufficiency. Woods, Gordon states:
The NEP document states, "it would be premature and unwise to count on the frontier to solve the oil supply problem". A CPA forecast (which does not include frontier production or new tar sands production) results in a shortfall of 740,000 barrels per day by 1990.
That is at least double, if not triple, the shortfall we have today.
As we continue, in spite of the fact that the Liberal government has almost turned consumption off-not because of conservation but because they have restrained business so much that they do not need any more-we have a situation now in which, if we were in full production of oil and doing what is possible, the shortfall that was feared in the last several years would still be apparent and real. The conservation measures which have been attempted are starting to have an impact now, and as much as hon. members opposite deny this in their remarks and their philosophy, the increased business price has had more to do with that than anything else. The Liberals fought an election on this and now they are again the happy beneficiaries of the fact that Canadians will turn to less use of oil and gas, and will use smaller cars because they cannot afford the prices which the Liberals have heaped upon them.
Another result of this so-called Canadianization program which has been undertaken has been a large outflow of capital from Canada. The figures vary but the latest figure I heard mentioned about a month ago about the outflow of capital from Canada was $10 billion, money which has gone to the United States and possibly other countries. This is a result of the effort to achieve more Canadian ownership. There has been an increase of Canadian content in the oil industry of from 27 per cent to 31 per cent. One of the serious consequences is the enormous pressure put on the Canadian dollar and the interest rates which this reflects. It is my hope that the Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen) has taken this situation into account, because it appears that the government has to slow that process down to reduce competition for capital in
Canada so that we do not face continuously the kind of economic pressure which our economy cannot stand today.
While the goal of increased Canadian ownership is admirable and one which would be supported by all sides of the House, the speed and amount of capital required to meet this goal is something the minister must take into account while doing his economic planning.
As this discussion culminates I think what we will see as the result of this program during the short time it has been in existence-approximately a year-is higher prices than we have anticipated. There has been no real improvement in our ability to be self-sufficient. There has been an aggravation to the economic recession we are in and Bill C-48 now takes us into an area in which the government is retroactively confiscating property.
This bill will increase ministerial discretion in the entire energy field. We have here a major move by the government to become intimately, aggressively and completely involved in the energy system in Canada. I would like to put that into the context of things that have happened over recent years in this country. That context has a very important message in terms of where this government is going and where the Canadian people can expect to be in the future if the government continues in power and on the same course it is on now.
In spite of the concern of New Democratic Party members that the government is not involved enough, through its budget the government is now more involved and taking more out of our gross national product than ever. It is more involved in a financial way than it has been at any time since the end of the Second World War. There has been a succession of measures taken by this government, which I am sure has been influenced enormously by senior civil servants. The government is involved in social programs to an extent never achieved before. The government is involved in health care and in all parts of the social system in an almost complete and total way, to the point where private involvement is very, very limited.
Now the government is involved in the energy system. Granted, it is involved just by way of introduction at the present time, but through this bill and the remainder of the National Energy Program there is the potential for almost total involvement. The government has the potential to control the entire energy system.
The final step)-and this is achieved through budgetary measures-is government involvement in business and the financing of small businesses and farmers all the way up to larger businesses and large corporations. I am sure hon. members opposite can respond to that, but I think the important proof of that is what happens in terms of the ability of the individual to own property. The Constitution has been the subject of a considerable amount of discussion lately, and I will not try to put this matter into that context; but there is no question that the ownership of property is not guaranteed by the Constitution.
December 9, 1981

There are some hon. members opposite who suggest that some of the budgetary measures were not a mistake but that they came at the wrong time; they are really what they wanted but at the wrong time. That is one point of view, but the more worrisome point of view is that those measures were not a mistake and really were designed and intended.
With respect to the ability of the individual to own property, I think some of the measures in the budget should be of major concern to all Canadians. I will not go into technical details, but I will mention the capital cost allowance changes, the changes in the capital gains tax, the changes in the incomeaveraging annuities and the changes respecting the ability of an individual to give a mortgage to somebody who wants to buy his business. Within a very few years all those changes will have the net result of making it almost impossible for an individual to buy a business or a farm. Those changes will make it undesirable for many people to retire on farms. There will be a tremendous impact on people who want to own property.
The government has taken the last step in the budget. It has taken the last major step into that wonderful world of socialism. Canadians across the country should recognize this and understand it. I suppose it is a cause for glee among some hon. members. While their motives are honest and while in their responses they can jest, what is happening is a tragedy.
If there are any examples of independent business left in this country, one is the example of independent cattlemen. They are the last free enterprisers. They do not have a marketing board. They have been doing their own thing. There are many who would accept marketing boards, there is no question about that, but the unfortunate thing is that they are looking for government grants. Businesses are looking for government grants. The government will have to provide grants in order to make it possible for people in this country to survive. Who will handle the grants? Who will tell the people who get grants what to do? I think there should be a major change. Perhaps there will be a tax revolt. It is clear that we in the official opposition will not get support from hon. members on my left, but perhaps we will be able to do something. It is unlikely that we can precipitate an election before its time, but there is a groundswell across the country. There is a gradual indication of discontent. Small business people are the first to make it known, along with insurance people and people who are feeling negative effects now. They understand the consequences of some of the measures in the budget.
I think Canadians want the self-respect and the dignity they should be able to earn. They want the tools to be able to function within a free enterprise economy. This government continues on its present course at its own peril. The Liberal caucus continues to support its Minister of Finance at its peril. I hope this situation can change soon. I am not completely in despair, and I am glad to have had this opportunity to express my concerns.

I shall review with hon. members the reasons for the government's conviction that this legislation and the management regime it establishes are essential to vigorous and responsible oil and gas development on the Canada lands.
Let us turn for a moment to the main elements of the new regime set out in Bill C-48. With respect to land management under Bill C-48, there will be stiffer work requirements through negotiated exploration agreements that include firm drilling commitments. The new management regime will provide a greater degree of control over the timing, direction, rate and level of exploration and development. This will be achieved through earlier release of proprietary information and prior approval of transfers and assignment of rights and drilling orders. The Bill also provides for ministerial authority to order production to commence and be delivered to Canadian markets in quantities and at prices specified in the order.
In terms of employment Bill C-48 will require, through negotiated exploration agreements, that companies submit detailed manpower plans which must include advance specification of labor requirements and sourcing, recruiting procedures, training programs and local hiring programs. Companies will need to establish and maintain close contact with the

December 9, 1981
Canada Oil and Gas Act
Canada Employment and Immigration Commission in the development and implementation of the plan. Thus we intend to ensure that Canadian workers have an opportunity to contribute their skills to developing oil and gas in the Canada lands. We will also require that the companies submit a procurement plan to ensure that Canadian manufacturers, consultants, contractors and service companies are given a full and fair opportunity to participate on a competitive basis in the supply of goods and services.
In the National Energy Program we were emphatic that decisions on energy development in the north would respond to the concerns of the native people. Despite this commitment, some native groups have expressed concern about Bill C-48, in part because they fear that development fostered by the new regime could prejudice their interest in land claims negotiations. The natives are asking us to prove our good intention.

speechtext:
As for protection of the environment, Bill C-48 will reinforce already stringent regulations and practice to ensure that the contribution of the Canada lands to Canada's energy security will not be at the expense of the environment.
Some elements of Bill C-48 relate to the fiscal regime for the Canada land that is intended to provide to all Canadians a share in the financial benefits flowing from the exploitation of their resources. The challenge here is to provide to investors a fair and competitive return on their investment, while at the same time ensuring a fair return to the Canadian people who own the land and who have supported exploration investments so generously through incentives on a scale available to no other industry.
First, as part of the over-all fiscal regime, a 25 per cent share of oil and gas production from the Canada lands will be reserved to the Crown. This share will be exercised through Petro-Canada or some other designated Crown corporation.
Second, to ensure that Canadians receive a fair return for their oil and gas resources, there will be a basic royalty of 10 per cent, with an additional royalty of 40 per cent of the net profits of the field above the 25 per cent rate of return.
December 9, 1981

Third, to provide the opportunity for direct Canadian participation there will be a minimum requirement of 50 per cent Canadian private and public sector ownership of production in the Canada lands.
In terms of price, the new oil reference price will promote a high level of exploration and development activity in the Canada lands. This generous pricing regime was established under the oil pricing and revenue-sharing agreement signed with the province of Alberta last September. By guaranteeing producers of new Canada lands oil world level prices, it recognizes that oil exploration and development on the frontiers are relatively high-cost, high-risk ventures.
In short, as industry has recognized, the new oil reference price makes Canada fully competitive in price terms with oil exploration and development anywhere in the world giving significant stimulus for Canada lands oil development as it does for new tar sands projects and for production from the remaining conventional oil prospects in western Canada.
Second, consider the fiscal incentive in the Canada lands in relation to other countries. After the incentives in the income tax system, even without the depletion allowance that will be in effect until 1985, the effective cost for a foreign-owned company exploring in the Canada lands is 53 cents on the dollar. This is lower than comparative figures for the U.S. offshore which range up to 67 cents on the dollar. This is without taking into account the fact that unlike the United States we have not required an up-front bonus bid. We know of no investment regime in any major producing country that is nearly as attractive.
Put another way, we consciously provide to foreign companies a regime that is more attractive to them than any they enjoy in their home country. As you know, the investment incentive for Canadian-owned companies is even richer, providing the basis for a wealth of prospective deals between major companies now holding most of the prospective land and Canadian companies wishing to participate.
Finally, consider returns to industry under the fiscal regime governing production. Recall for a moment the numbers submitted by Petro-Canada. Using a sample field, Petro-Canada calculated that international investors would earn a rate of return of 24.4 per cent in the United Kingdom, 18.3 per cent in Norway, 21.6 per cent in the United States, not counting the bonus bids, and as much as 27.7 per cent in Canada. Together, the lower cost of investment on the Canada lands, our world level prices for new oil and exciting oil prospects provide the industry with prospective returns that are very attractive by U.S., U.K., Norwegian or any other standard. I know of no company which has taken the trouble to compare the economics in the Canada lands to regimes elsewhere that will debate this point. The numbers are there. They are public knowledge. Any analyst can verify them.
I want to address some of the specific criticisms which have been directed towards the Crown interest provision. Critics of the Crown share have called it an "expropriation" or a "land
Canada Oil and Gas Act
grab". They have been especially critical of the fact that the Crown interest will apply retroactively, as it applies to all lands not currently in production, whether or not exploration and discoveries have already taken place. They also continue to claim a right to substantial compensation. Mr. Speaker, this reaction stems from a basic misunderstanding of the Crown interest and its role established by Bill C-48.
The Crown interest involves retention by the Crown of 25 per cent of all interest in the Canada lands, except those where production has already occurred. The government also is involved directly in the management of the venture, commensurate with the level of its share. In return, the Crown will contribute 25 per cent of all costs involved. To argue that the Crown interest is a carried interest, a "free-ride", is obviously a misportrayal. We are paying for all of our share through the 25 per cent Crown interest incentive payment, by carrying our share of costs at the development stage, the Crown's interest is carried up to the point when a production plan is filed, at which point the Crown must convert its holdings to a working interest.
There are circumstances where the Crown might elect to convert to a working interest before exploration is completed, in which case the other partners would be paid double for the Crown's share of the costs, first through the 25 per cent Crown interest incentive payment, and second through a proportionate contribution by the Crown's working interest agent. In any event, the Crown will always contribute its share of the cost of developing a field for production. This activity usually accounts for 85 per cent or more of the total investment.
It is important to see Crown interest and its application in the proper context. First of all, it represents a means by which all Canadians can share in the benefits of a resource that is and will remain 100 per cent owned by Canadians. Canadians have, through their tax dollars, paid for the majority of the oil and gas exploration work. Moreover, the principle of Crown interest is not a new development; it incorporates elements of Canadian energy policy which have been evolving for the last 20 years.
Since the establishment of the Canada oil and gas land regulations in 1961, the world and the place of energy in it have changed. The Crown interest provision is one of the means, along with royalties, of ensuring that Canadians share in the benefits of the greatly increased value of the energy resources in the Canada lands.
Let us be quite clear on one point. The new regime, whatever its form, inevitably had to result in a greater government share of oil and gas revenues than would have been the case under the existing rules or the rules proposed in 1977. Existing rights were issued prior to the 1979 explosion in world oil prices and most lands now held by the industry even pre-date the emergence of OPEC's radical pricing policies in 1974.
These OPEC actions transformed the world oil market and effected a huge windfall economic gain on existing reserves and oil and gas rights. Canada has, as has every other government faced with this situation-including Norway, the United Kingdom and even the United States-made it clear that this

December 9, 1981
Canada Oil and Gas Act
windfall would not accrue to the industry alone. On the Canada lands, the larger federal revenues from under the 25 per cent Crown interest and the progressive incremental royalty are intended to achieve government revenue objectives and can be equated reasonably to the fiscal measures of the United Kingdom and the United States, which have dramatically increased government revenues from existing reserves of oil and gas.
It is essential to establish this point quite early. There is an obligation upon us, as stewards of this national resource, to establish a mix of measures that give both the industry and the owners of the resource a fair share. On the basis of our comparative analysis of international regimes, we came to the conclusion that the regime had to be substantially toughened up, even over the 1977 rules, if we were to fulfil our responsibilities. Thus, it was not a question of a Crown interest or not; it was a question, with us, of how we would obtain this magnitude of share. Each country has its own approach.
Let me illustrate this with a United States example. In 1979, the United States, having decontrolled oil prices, imposed a tax called the "windfall profits tax". It applied to all production, current and future. It provided for a tax ranging from 30 per cent to 70 per cent on production profits. Quite clearly, to a dramatic extent, this affected the value of the industry's already discovered assets. Yet so far as we can ascertain, no serious attempt was made by companies in the United States to obtain compensation for this measure, which was every bit as retroactive as the Crown interest provision. Indeed, it was much more retroactive, because we are grandfathering existing production in the Canada lands. There are literally dozens of similar examples from around the world and within Canada.
For example, consider Alberta. A former cabinet minister of the Alberta government, the Hon. Bill Yurko, had this to say in the House of Commons on November 3, 1981, as reported at page 12460 of Hansard:
I want to say first that I was involved as a minister of a government for over half a dozen years in changing drastically the energy regime in Alberta. No one has to tell me about retroactive legislation. We changed every lease in Alberta retroactively and changed the royalty structure from a maximum 16% per cent to a much higher royalty.

Indeed, we changed legislation to effectively change the transfer of ownership of oil and gas.
Yet no company, so far as we know, claimed compensation for this retroactive change of rules affecting existing reserves.
Against this background, it is unreasonable to claim that the Crown interest does something more to the industry's assets than other fiscal measures, here and elsewhere, have done time
and again, as governments took steps to ensure that their citizens obtained a fair share of the gains from the increased value of oil and gas production.
It is time we lay to rest the claim that the Crown interest is a measure that is financially unusual or that it calls for compensation. Consider the options we had at our disposal to ensure that Canadians got a fair share of profits from resources that they, not the oil companies, own. We could, for example, have raised the basic royalty, say to levels prevailing in Alberta. This would have raised it, on average, by 25 or 30 percentage points. The Crown's share of Canada lands production then would have been at least 35 to 40 per cent in the form of a royalty. This would have been more onerous on the industry than the Crown interest provision will be. For one thing, we pay our full share of costs in return for the Crown share. Yet I get the impression that had we opted for a royalty solution, the protests from the industry and from other governments would have been less intense.
Particular attention has been focused on the Crown interest in Hibernia, where Petro-Canada already had acquired an interest in the play in 1979 by virtue of the so-called back-in provision. It has been proposed that, because of this back-in, the Crown interest provision of Bill C-48 should not apply to Hibernia. Canadian ownership in that venture reached 35 per cent. Surely it would be inequitable to apply the Crown interest to those permit holders that actively sought private Canadian participation, but not to Hibernia. We can see no special case for the Hibernia partners. Their return will still be higher than they can earn in the other countries to which I have referred.
The new regime for the Canada lands leaves foreign-owned companies with an investment return that is superior to that available in their home countries. Consider for a moment a situation where Petro-Canada is involved in development in, say, Norway. If Norway were, in a reasonable and even-handed fashion, to change the fiscal rules, would anyone plausibly argue that such a move warranted protests on the part of the Canadian government? The case for protest would become even less sustainable if the new regime still left Petro-Canada better off-
